Yes, you're right, and it's not pedantry: the two numbers can differ by a lot.

A p-value of 0.03 is P(data this extreme | null true). The claim "97% chance the hypothesis is true" is P(hypothesis | data), which also depends on the prior plausibility of the hypothesis and on the power of the test. Flipping the conditional is the prosecutor's fallacy.

The gap is large in practice. Under the Sellke-Bayarri-Berger calibration, p = 0.03 corresponds to a Bayes factor against the null of at most about 3.5:1. Even starting from a generous 50/50 prior, the null retains at least about 22% posterior probability, not 3%. With a skeptical prior (most tested hypotheses being false), it is far higher.

If your colleague wants a one-line version: p = 0.03 means "if there were no effect, data like this would be rare," not "there's probably an effect."
